video_title: Will AI Rout Cause A Recession & A Bear Market?
gist: Ed Yardeni and colleagues argue last week's AI-led rout was a valuation-driven bull market correction, not a recession-driven bear market: earnings estimates kept rising while Nvidia, semis and the Mag 7 de-rated to bear-market multiples, and Friday likely marked the low. They trimmed the year-end S&P 500 target to 7,500 on a lower P/E, still call for a 50bp December Fed hike, and moved global equities to market weight.

themes.theme: AI sell-off: multiple compression, not earnings

insights.claim: Yardeni Research concluded last week's AI-led sell-off was driven by contracting valuation multiples, while consensus earnings estimates kept rising above the firm's own 2027 and 2028 targets.
insights.speaker: Elias (Yardeni Research)
insights.so_what: Sell-offs driven by P/E de-rating with rising estimates have historically been buyable; watch whether estimate revisions turn down before treating it as a fundamental bear.
insights.quote: what really drove the sell off last week was this ongoing contraction in valuation multiples

insights.claim: In 2018 and 2022 multiples contracted sharply while earnings estimates held up, and the slowdown implied by the de-rating never materialized, making both episodes great buying opportunities; Yardeni sees the current setup as the same pattern.
insights.speaker: Elias (Yardeni Research)
insights.so_what: Use the 2018/2022 analog: if the economy doesn't slow as much as multiples imply, P/E mean-reverts upward.

insights.claim: Ed Yardeni characterized the drop as a 'bull market correction' rather than a tech-wreck bear market, noting bear markets normally accompany recessions and he sees no recession (2022 being the exception).
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Base case stays a bull market through the 'roaring 2020s'; recession signals, not price action, would change the call.
insights.quote: it was a bull market correction and it's probably over

insights.claim: Yardeni wrote in a Monday morning quick take, before the Jensen Huang news broke, that Friday November 20 may have marked the low, with the S&P 500 finding support around 7,000 after breaking below its two-year uptrend and 200-day moving average.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Watch ~7,000 on the S&P 500 as the key support level (also the pre-war level).

insights.claim: The S&P 500 large-cap forward P/E fell to 16.4 and the Magnificent 7 forward P/E broke below 20 on November 20, levels lower than on Liberation Day and near the 2022 bear-market lows.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Valuations at bear-market-low levels without a recession argue for accumulating large caps.
insights.quote: the Mag 7 broke below 20. The large caps were down to 16.4

insights.claim: The growth-to-value forward P/E ratio collapsed back to about 1, meaning investors were no longer paying any premium for growth, which Yardeni reads as a likely bottom.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A growth/value P/E ratio near 1 has marked bottoms for growth relative performance.

insights.claim: Credit markets did not confirm the equity panic: the VIX and Nasdaq VIX rose but high-yield bond yields barely moved, whereas true recession/bear crashes show high-yield yields going straight up.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Use high-yield yields as the confirmation signal; equity vol spikes without credit stress are likely corrections.

insights.claim: Nvidia's forward P/E fell to 8.1 during the rout, back to the multiple it carried when it was purely a gaming company, which Yardeni called an amazing buying opportunity.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Extreme de-rating in the AI leader with intact earnings was the clearest dip-buy of the episode.
insights.quote: So it got back to being a gaming company

insights.claim: The semiconductor index forward P/E dropped to 9.4 on November 20 (a chart showed 11.1 in error), about as cheap as semis get historically.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Semis at single-digit forward multiples offer asymmetric upside if AI capex merely slows rather than collapses.

insights.claim: A rally followed President Trump reportedly calling Nvidia's board to bring back Jensen Huang; Yardeni argues Trump intervenes whenever the market (and his portfolio) falls, acting as a de facto plunge-protection mechanism.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Political intervention risk skews downside tails shorter; but it also adds unpredictability ('so is President Donald Trump').
insights.quote: whenever the market goes down, he does something to make it go up

insights.claim: Yardeni's 8,500-9,000 S&P 500 target for end-2027 does not depend on Jensen Huang's return or any AI upside surprise, only that the AI trade does not go into a tailspin.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The bull case requires only a slower AI build-out, not acceleration.

insights.claim: Yardeni suggests a slower AI build-out may reveal the semiconductor shortage is less intense than Jensen Huang claimed when urging customers to buy chips.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Watch for softening chip-shortage narratives as a risk to semiconductor pricing power.

themes.theme: Three pillars of US economic resilience

insights.claim: Yardeni's resilience thesis rests on three pillars: a consumer supported by an improving labor market and the wealth effect, a continuing (if slower) AI build-out, and a government running a ~6% of GDP ($2 trillion) deficit during an expansion.
insights.speaker: Elias (Yardeni Research)
insights.so_what: A recession would require multiple pillars to fail, not just AI.

insights.claim: Financial, political and social constraints on AI are 'speed bumps, not roadblocks', and Yardeni sees a slower AI build-out as healthy because speed bumps reduce accidents, with bond and credit markets regulating the pace.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Expect decelerating but continuing AI capex; credit spreads are the governor to monitor.

insights.claim: Yardeni rejects the view that the economy is entirely AI-driven and that an AI implosion would sink it, arguing data centers under construction will still be built rather than turned into pickleball facilities.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Pushback on the consensus 'AI-or-bust' macro narrative.

insights.claim: Retiring baby boomers keep spending and are financially helping their young-adult children through an affordability crisis, supporting consumer resilience.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Wealth-effect-driven boomer spending supports consumer discretionary demand even as younger cohorts are squeezed.

insights.claim: Roughly $1 trillion of federal net interest payments flows to households and others, making the large deficit significantly stimulative even as it is a fiscal problem.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Higher rates partly self-offset via interest income, sustaining demand and inflation pressure.
insights.quote: The trillion dollars of net interest payments are going to somebody

insights.claim: Yardeni expects a 50 basis point Fed funds hike at the December FOMC versus a 25bp consensus, viewing last year's 75bp of cuts as mistakes that must be reversed; it estimates neutral at 4.25%-4.5%.
insights.speaker: Elias (Yardeni Research)
insights.so_what: Positioned for a more hawkish Fed than consensus; front-end yields at risk if the 50bp call is right.
insights.quote: our neutral rate estimate is between 4 and 1/4 and 4 and 1/2 %

insights.claim: Elias argues the Fed should not react to short-term equity volatility or falling copper and gasoline prices, and that structural inflation still requires further tightening.
insights.speaker: Elias (Yardeni Research)
insights.so_what: Don't count on a 'Fed put' from the equity drawdown.

insights.claim: Commodities signal moderating inflation, but the Cleveland Fed nowcast shows October and November inflation running above 3% year-over-year, far from the 2% target; November CPI relief from gasoline will arrive only after the December FOMC.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Inflation data timing favors a hawkish December decision.
insights.quote: they're all going to have three handles on a year-over-year percent basis

insights.claim: Yardeni cut its year-end S&P 500 target from 7,900 to 7,500, keeping $425 forward EPS for next year but lowering the forward P/E from 18.6 to 17.6, its second target cut this year (from an earlier 8,400).
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Target cut is valuation-only; earnings view unchanged. Santa Claus rally back to 7,900 would be welcomed.

insights.claim: Yardeni keeps 8,500-9,000 for the S&P 500 next year and 10,000 by the end of the decade.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Long-run bull framework intact through the 'roaring 2020s'.

insights.claim: S&P 500 Q3 earnings growth was 27.1% and Q4 is expected at 30% excluding mark-to-market gains; Q3 earnings dipped only because of smaller mark-to-market gains at Amazon and Alphabet, and Q4 may see large gains tied to Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Underlying operating earnings momentum is very strong; watch for Anthropic-related mark-to-market boosts in Q4.
insights.quote: I guess we're going to have some huge gains with Anthropic in the fourth quarter

insights.claim: Analysts' forward, 2027 and 2028 earnings estimates kept rising to record highs even during last week's sell-off, a pattern last seen in 2004-2006, unlike the downward revisions of 2001-2003.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Rising estimate revisions during a drawdown signal a correction, not an earnings recession.

themes.theme: Global equities: back to market weight

insights.claim: Yardeni moved from overweight 'go global' to market weight about a month ago because the US and MSCI World ex US have tracked each other closely in performance, earnings and forward margins.
insights.speaker: Toby Hurst
insights.so_what: No regional tilt for now; market weight already means a very large US allocation.

insights.claim: The US-versus-global forward P/E spread narrowed to 6.5 points from above 9 in 2024, though Asia, especially Korea and Taiwan, has been hit harder in the valuation reset.
insights.speaker: Toby Hurst
insights.so_what: Narrower US premium reduces the valuation case for international, but volatile Asian markets offer dip-buys.

insights.claim: MSCI Korea's forward P/E fell to 3.2 as of Thursday's close, a level Toby Hurst said has basically never happened historically.
insights.speaker: Toby Hurst
insights.so_what: Extreme Korean valuation could be a deep-value contrarian opportunity.
insights.quote: the MSCI Korea forward PE was down to uh 3.2 which if you look historically basically has never happened

insights.claim: Global yields have risen alongside the roughly 80bp rise in the US 10-year in recent months; Australia has the second-highest policy rate among 41 developed nations per the IMF, and protests in Spain and France pushed up European yields.
insights.speaker: Toby Hurst
insights.so_what: Global bond pressure is synchronized; the US is not unique in its rate problem.

insights.claim: Australia and New Zealand often lead global rates and central bank policy; New Zealand recently held rates despite a 95% market-implied probability of a hike, though the team doubts the Fed will follow suit.
insights.speaker: Toby Hurst
insights.so_what: Watch Antipodean central banks as an early read on global policy turns.
